summary: Specifies algorithms for encoding or hashing an arbitrary string to a point on an elliptic curve. This is a building block for many cryptographic protocols. It is a product of the Crypto Forum Research Group.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a recipe for turning any message into a specific spot on a special curve, which many secret-code systems need.

subtitle: Algorithms for encoding arbitrary strings to points on elliptic curves.

tldr.problem: Many cryptographic protocols need a way to hash arbitrary data to points on an elliptic curve, but doing this correctly is subtle. Naive approaches leak timing information or produce biased outputs.
tldr.mechanism: Hash the input to field elements using expand_message, deterministically map field elements to curve points, then clear the cofactor to land in the prime-order subgroup.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can hash to elliptic curves in constant time, suitable for protocols like password-authenticated key exchange, identity-based encryption, and verifiable random functions.

today: RFC 9380 is an Informational RFC that represents the consensus of the Crypto Forum Research Group. It is actively used in many cryptographic protocols including password-authenticated key exchanges, identity-based encryption schemes, and consensus protocols. Implementations exist in major cryptographic libraries, and the specifications are production-ready.

sections.title: Introduction and Applications
sections.content:
Many cryptographic protocols require a procedure that encodes an arbitrary input, such as a password or a protocol message, to a point on an elliptic curve. Examples include password-authenticated key exchanges (like SPAKE2), identity-based encryption, Boneh-Lynn-Shacham signatures, verifiable random functions, and oblivious pseudorandom functions.

The challenge is that hashing to elliptic curves is subtle. Naive implementations can leak timing information about the input or produce biased outputs that weaken security. This RFC specifies algorithms that provide constant-time implementations, suitable for deployment in sensitive applications. The document provides specific recommendations for widely used curves (NIST P-256, P-384, P-521; curve25519; edwards25519; curve448; edwards448; secp256k1; and BLS12-381) and guidance for implementing custom curves.
sections.plainLanguage: Many secret-code systems need to turn any piece of data into a point on a special curve. This RFC is a cookbook for doing it safely, without leaking secrets through timing.

sections.title: The Three-Step Approach
sections.content:
All hash-to-curve constructions in this document follow three steps: hash to field elements, deterministic mapping to curve points, and cofactor clearing.

The hash_to_field function takes an arbitrary message and a domain separation tag (DST) and produces one or more uniformly random field elements. To avoid statistical bias, it uses enough output bits: for a field of size p, it computes ceil(log2(p)) + k bits, where k is the target security level (typically 128 bits). This ensures the bias after modular reduction is negligibly small.

The map_to_curve function takes a field element and outputs a point on the elliptic curve. Different mappings are optimized for different curve families: Shallue-van de Woestijne for Weierstrass curves, Elligator 2 for Montgomery and Edwards curves. These mappings are deterministic and can be implemented in constant time.

The clear_cofactor function moves any point on the curve to the prime-order subgroup G, which is required for cryptographic security. For most curves, this is a simple scalar multiplication.
sections.plainLanguage: The process has three steps: (1) hash the message into field numbers, (2) use those numbers to calculate a point on the curve, (3) move that point to the secure subgroup.

sections.title: Two Encodings: Nonuniform and Uniform
sections.content:
This RFC defines two compositions of the three basic functions, suited to different applications.

encode_to_curve is the simpler and faster encoding. It hashes the message to a single field element, maps it to a curve point, and clears the cofactor. The output is nonuniform: not every point in the prime-order subgroup is equally likely, and many points cannot be output. This is acceptable in some protocols but not in others.

hash_to_curve is the stronger encoding for protocols proven secure in the random-oracle model. It hashes the message to two field elements, maps each to a point, adds the points together, and clears the cofactor. The output is statistically close to uniform over the prime-order subgroup. This uniformity is essential for protocols where the adversary can choose the input after observing other outputs.

Both encodings include a domain separation tag (DST) in the hash_to_field computation. This ensures that different uses of the same curves in different protocols do not interfere with each other's security proofs, a concern that arises when analyzing protocols in the random-oracle model.
sections.plainLanguage: The faster recipe (encode_to_curve) skips a step but produces points that are not spread evenly across the curve. The stronger recipe (hash_to_curve) does extra work to guarantee the output is as randomly distributed as possible.

sections.title: Deterministic Mapping Algorithms
sections.content:
The core of this RFC is a set of deterministic mappings from field elements to elliptic curve points. Different mappings are optimized for different curve families.

For Weierstrass curves (the most common form y^2 = x^3 + Ax + B), three methods are provided. The Shallue-van de Woestijne method is the most generic; it works on any Weierstrass curve. The Simplified Shallue-van de Woestijne-Ulas (SWU) method is faster for most curves, requiring fewer operations and a smaller number of square roots. The Simplified SWU for AB == 0 variant handles special curves like secp256k1 and BLS12-381 by mapping through an isogenous curve.

For Montgomery curves (the form used in curve25519 and curve448), the Elligator 2 method is recommended. It is efficient and works for the parameters of these widely-used curves.

For twisted Edwards curves (edwards25519, edwards448), the mapping uses Elligator 2 on an equivalent Montgomery curve, then converts the result back to Edwards form via a rational map.

All mappings are designed to be implementable in constant time: their execution time and memory access patterns do not depend on the input, preventing timing side-channel attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Different types of curves need different recipes for turning a field number into a point. The RFC provides recipes for the most common curve families, chosen for both speed and security.

sections.title: Security and Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations MUST avoid rejection sampling (try-and-increment methods), which are hard to make constant-time. Instead, this RFC uses deterministic algorithms that always produce a valid output on the first try.

Constant-time implementation is critical: all arithmetic, comparisons, and square roots must run in time independent of the input values. This prevents attackers from learning information about the input by measuring how long the hash-to-curve operation takes. The RFC provides helper functions like is_square and sqrt with guidance on constant-time implementations, and includes Appendix I with algorithms for square roots on various fields.

Domain separation is mandatory. Every invocation of hash_to_curve or encode_to_curve MUST use a distinct domain separation tag (DST). This is typically constructed as "ApplicationName-Version-Ciphersuite-CurveID", with a minimum length of 16 bytes. Domain separation ensures that if a protocol uses multiple hashes to the same curve, or if the same curve is used in different protocols, the hashes produce independent random oracles.

Field operations, especially inversion, must handle edge cases carefully. The RFC provides the inv0 function that returns 0 when inverting 0, which simplifies exception handling.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementations must carefully handle edge cases, use constant-time arithmetic to prevent timing leaks, and label each use of the function so different applications do not interfere with each other.

sections.title: Recommended Hash-to-Curve Suites
sections.content:
This RFC provides complete, ready-to-use suite specifications for hashing to widely-deployed curves. Each suite specifies the field, the curve equation, the mapping function, the hash function for message expansion (typically SHA-256 or SHA-512 via expand_message_xmd, or SHAKE128/SHAKE256 via expand_message_xof), the cofactor clearing method, and serialization formats.

For NIST curves (P-256, P-384, P-521), the Simplified SWU mapping is recommended, using either SHA-2 hash functions or SHAKE with XOF. For curve25519 and edwards25519, Elligator 2 is recommended with SHA-512 and expand_message_xmd. For curve448 and edwards448, Elligator 2 with SHAKE256 and expand_message_xof is recommended. For secp256k1, the Simplified SWU method with an isogeny map is used. For BLS12-381 (a pairing-friendly curve used in many protocols), Simplified SWU with isogeny maps for both G1 and G2 are provided.

Implementors choosing an existing suite SHOULD use the recommended option for the target curve. Applications that need a custom curve not in this document SHOULD follow the guidelines in Section 8.9 to define a new suite, including appropriate choices of mapping, expansion function, and hash function.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC provides ready-made recipes for all the common curves used in real protocols. Implementors can look up their curve and use the specified algorithm.
